ch02.note: Fourth Avenue (四马路), today Fuzhou Road, was a street of the International Settlement famous for its bookshops, teahouses, theaters and newspaper offices, and notorious for its brothels. The produce market of these opening scenes was a real building at the Fuzhou–Zhejiang Road corner, completed in 1930 and among the most modern in the city; the library on its upper floors, with the disused room behind the stacks, is where the meeting is laid. (Corroborated.)

The Zhejiang Grand Theater (浙江大戏院), on Zhejiang Road directly facing the market, was a real Art Deco cinema of 1930 — the first Shanghai theater by the Hungarian architect László Hudec (邬达克), whose buildings recur through these chapters. (Corroborated.)

The Shanghai Municipal Council (工部局) governed the foreign-run International Settlement, and its own force, the Municipal Police, policed it. Because the Nationalists' Longhua garrison had no lawful power to make arrests inside the Settlement, it had to work through the Council's police; that jurisdictional seam runs through the whole of the arrest. (Corroborated.)

ch02.anchor: The amusement ground had a forlorn look
ch02.note: The World Hotel (世界大旅社), with its roof-garden amusement ground overlooking the market, is one of the story's Shanghai settings; rooftop pleasure gardens of this kind were a real feature of the Fourth Avenue district, though the sources consulted differ on whether this particular hotel is documented. It is not the famous Great World (大世界) amusement arcade. (Uncorroborated.)

The Lyceum Theatre (兰心大戏院), the Settlement's principal Western theater and home of its British amateur dramatic society, is given here by its standing English name; the building of these years, opened in 1931, still stands on today's Maoming Road South. (Corroborated.)

Cuckoo Soul Abroad (海外鹃魂) was an early 1930s film of the Lianhua company; its star Jin Yan (金焰), a Korea-born actor hailed as the 'Emperor of Film,' played opposite the actress Ziluolan. In classical verse the cuckoo (杜鹃) is said to weep blood for grief, which sharpens Wei Dafu's joke that all three leads end up dead. (Jin Yan and the Lianhua title are corroborated; the film's exact cast is not.)

Longhua (龙华), southwest of the city, was the seat of the Songhu (Shanghai–Woosung) Garrison Command and its prison, beside the Longhua Temple and its ancient pagoda. In February 1931 the Nationalists secretly shot some two dozen Communists here—the 'Longhua Martyrs,' among them the 'Five Martyrs' of the League of Left-Wing Writers (Rou Shi, Hu Yepin, Yin Fu, Feng Keng and Li Weisen), a killing mourned by Lu Xun. It is to this garrison that the prisoners of the novel are taken. (Corroborated.)

The Generalissimo (委员长) is Chiang Kai-shek (蒋介石, 1887–1975), chairman of the Nationalist Military Affairs Commission and head of the KMT government and army. In the winter of 1932–33, the novel's moment, he was directing the Fourth Encirclement Campaign against the Communists' Central Soviet. (Corroborated.)

Mount Lu (庐山, Lushan), above Jiujiang in Jiangxi, was the Nationalist government's summer seat, where Chiang Kai-shek kept a villa and transacted business of state; a petitioner such as Du Yuesheng seeking the Generalissimo's ear would indeed go up the mountain. (Corroborated.)

The China Merchants Steam Navigation Company (招商局), founded by the Qing statesman Li Hongzhang (here 'Grand Secretary Li'), was at the center of a real 1933 scandal. Li's grandson Li Guojie (李国杰), who ran one of its arms, was accused of mortgaging the company's Shanghai wharves—among them the Jinliyuan of the earlier scene—for a vast loan and pocketing the kickback, with Chen Fumu (陈孚木) as a go-between; a Shanghai court sentenced Li to eight years in April 1933. The gangster Du Yuesheng (the 'tycoon Du') hovers behind the affair as the detectives gossip it. (Corroborated; Du's exact role is not settled by the sources.)

ch02.anchor: The fifteenth of the last month of the year
ch02.note: The fifteenth of the last month of the year renders 腊月十五, a date in 腊月 (layue), the twelfth and last month of the Chinese lunar calendar, whose close brings the New Year. The novel opens in the days before the Lunar New Year, which in 1933 fell on January 26; almost the whole action of the book plays out across that turn of the year. (Corroborated.)

Baiyunguan (白云观), the 'White Cloud' Daoist temple in the old Chinese city, gave its name to a nearby base and lock-up of the Songhu Garrison Command's detective squad; real prisoners were held there, among them the leader Deng Yanda (邓演达) in 1931. It is from this Nanshi post, not from Longhua, that the squad musters. (Corroborated.)

Nanshi (南市, 'the southern market') was the old walled Chinese city and its district, south of the foreign concessions and under Chinese administration; its police were a Chinese force ('one of our own, placed there') separate from the Settlement's Municipal Police and the French Concession's own—one of the three jurisdictions whose seams the underground works. (Corroborated.)

Suzhou Creek (苏州河), the tidal lower course of the Wusong River, winds through the north of the city to meet the Huangpu; it was old Shanghai's working waterway, and the market's fresh produce comes down it by boat each morning. (Corroborated.)

The Gezhi Public School (格致公学) was a real English-style boys' school in the central International Settlement, run by the Municipal Council (工部局) from 1917—the former Chinese Polytechnic (格致书院) taken under foreign management. It survives today as the Gezhi Middle School. (Corroborated.)

The orchestra Qin Chuan'an comes to hear rehearse is the Shanghai Municipal Orchestra (工部局乐队), the ensemble kept up by the Municipal Council of the International Settlement; under its Italian conductor Mario Paci (梅百器) it was reckoned the finest orchestra in the Far East, and gave its concerts at the Town Hall and the Lyceum Theatre. That it should rehearse here in the World Hotel is the novel's own placement. (The orchestra corroborated; the venue the novel's.)

ch02.anchor: kept a gramophone in his own clinic
ch02.note: A gramophone and a shelf of records were, in 1933, the mark of a Westernized man of means; Qin Chuan'an's, recurring through the book, is of a piece with his German-hospital training and his taste for the orchestra. (Texture.)

Indanthrene blue (阴丹士林) was a German synthetic vat dye, discovered by the BASF chemist René Bohn in 1901 and far more colorfast than indigo; the cloth dyed with it, heavily advertised in China from the late 1920s, became the signature deep blue of students' and scholars' long gowns and of the qipao. (Corroborated.)

The Central Police Station (中央捕房), on Foochow Road, was the headquarters of the Shanghai Municipal Police, the force of the foreign-run International Settlement; its many Chinese detectives, of whom Detective Yao is one, did the ground-level work and dealt directly with the Nationalist services. (Corroborated.)

The Political Branch is the Shanghai Municipal Police's Special Branch (established 1925), the Settlement force's political-intelligence arm, which kept extensive files on the Communists and the Comintern. (Corroborated.)

The passage describes a real accommodation. Through the later 1920s and early 1930s the Shanghai Municipal Police worked with the Nationalist authorities to share intelligence and to hand over—extradite—arrested Communists from the Settlement to Chinese jurisdiction. Because the Longhua garrison could not lawfully make arrests inside the foreign Settlement, this cooperation is what makes the whole operation possible. (Corroborated.)

The Judge Advocate's office (军法处) was the military-justice department of the Songhu (Shanghai–Woosung) Garrison Command, set up in 1928; it tried 'political' and Communist cases outside the ordinary courts and ran the detentions and executions at Longhua. You Tianxiao's detective squad operates under it. (Corroborated.)

ch02.anchor: once they had joined the action group
ch02.note: An action group (行动小组) was a task cell assembled for one operation from comrades of different lines, who were required to break with their former work and know only one another; the compartmentalization is a security measure, and the reason the arrested strangers can betray so little. (Texture.)

The Hatchet Gang (斧头帮) was the assassination network of the Anhui-born Wang Yaqiao (王亚樵); its gunmen really did shoot Zhao Tieqiao (赵铁桥), general manager of the China Merchants Steam Navigation Company, at the company's door on July 24, 1930. That Li Guojie set the killing on, amid the struggle for control of the company, is the received account rather than a documented fact. (The gang and the killing corroborated; Li's part uncorroborated.)

ch02.anchor: laid a hand on the tiger's backside
ch02.note: To have laid a hand on the tiger's backside renders 摸老虎屁股, to provoke someone too powerful and dangerous to be crossed with impunity. (Idiom.)
Fish and dragons mingled renders 鱼龙混杂, an idiom for a place where the worthy and the worthless, honest men and rogues, are all thrown in together. (Idiom.)

Pai gow (牌九, 'make nine') is a gambling game played with a set of thirty-two Chinese dominoes (骨牌); the comrades' cover is that each has brought a few dominoes and they are assembling a set between them. That the dominoes serve as the meeting's recognition tokens, and the dice as the sign of the man 'sent from above,' is the mechanism the whole plot turns on. (Corroborated.)

ch02.anchor: a bowl of soybean milk and a hunk of fried flatbread
ch02.note: A bowl of soybean milk (豆浆) with a hunk of fried flatbread (大饼), and the sesame cakes below, are the classic street breakfast of Shanghai and the lower Yangtze; Cui Wentai's whim for a bowl of pork-offal soup instead is the small human swerve that will undo him. (Texture.)

ch03.note: The Central Party Affairs Investigation Section (党务调查科) was the Kuomintang's political-intelligence organ, run under the Central Organization Department by the Chen brothers' 'CC Clique' and from 1929 by Xu Enzeng; those in the know called its Nanjing base, in the Zhanyuan garden, the 'Special Operations Headquarters.' It was the forerunner of the wartime Bureau of Investigation and Statistics (中统). You Tianxiao's secret post in it, outranking his open one, is the source of his double-dealing. (Corroborated.)

ch03.anchor: the 32nd Army of the National Revolutionary Army
ch03.note: A 32nd Army of the National Revolutionary Army did exist, but it was Shang Zhen's (商震) Shanxi–Suiyuan force, stationed in Hebei in 1931–33, not at Shanghai; the units that actually held Longhua under the Songhu Garrison Command were others. Posting a '32nd Army' to the Shanghai garrison is the novel's own detail, not the historical record. (Contradicted.)

The pagoda beside the garrison is the ancient Longhua Pagoda, standardly 龙华塔; Bao'en Pagoda (报恩塔, 'Pagoda of Requited Kindness') is a genuine traditional alternate name for it, from the legend that Sun Quan of Wu raised it to repay his mother. The source thus uses a historically valid variant, not a mistake. (Corroborated.)

Xi Shi (西施), a legendary beauty of the state of Yue in the Spring and Autumn era, was by tradition sent to beguile the king of rival Wu and hasten its ruin—the archetypal planted agent. As a cryptonym for a mole inside the enemy's ranks it is pointed; the identity of 'Xi Shi' is one of the book's central secrets.

ch03.anchor: the Blue Sky and White Sun flag
ch03.note: The Blue Sky and White Sun flag is the national flag of the Republic of China under the Nationalists—a white twelve-rayed sun on a blue canton over a red field (青天白日满地红), adopted in 1928; the blue-sky-white-sun emblem is also the Kuomintang's own party flag. Its flying over the gate marks the ground as Nationalist military territory. (Corroborated.)

Longhua Temple (龙华寺), beside the garrison, is the oldest and largest of Shanghai's Buddhist temples—its founding traditionally ascribed to Sun Quan of Wu in the third century, its pagoda dating to 977—and is famous for its spring peach blossoms and temple fair. The killing-ground sits in the shadow of this ancient sanctuary. (Corroborated.)

To murmur Amitābha (阿弥陀佛) is to invoke the Buddha of the Western Paradise; the phrase is a reflexive pious ejaculation, said much as an English speaker might sigh 'Lord have mercy.' Here it is a reflex of habit as Mu Chuan glances at the pagoda, with an irony the reader is left to feel. (Texture.)

ch03.anchor: The Theory and Practice of Secret-Service Work
ch03.note: The Theory and Practice of Secret-Service Work lightly renames a real text. After the Communist security chief Gu Shunzhang (顾顺章) defected to the Nationalists in 1931, he wrote up the underground's methods in works such as The Theory and Practice of Special-Service Work (特务工作的理论与实际), which became training manuals for the Nationalist secret services. That You Tianxiao must apply, through channels, for a guarded copy is true to the book's restricted circulation. (Corroborated.)

The Zhanyuan garden (瞻园) in Nanjing, into which the Investigation Section moved, is a celebrated Ming classical garden—the west garden of the mansion of Xu Da (徐达), foremost general of the Ming founding, and later the palace of the Taiping 'Eastern King'; today it houses the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom History Museum. That the Nationalists' secret police kept their 'Special Operations Headquarters' in so storied a garden is historical fact. (Corroborated.)

Badger-game swindlers renders 仙人跳: a con in which a woman lures a man and a confederate, posing as her wronged husband, bursts in to extort him. The trick is old, attested from the Song under other names and called 仙人跳 by Qing times. (Corroborated.)

The Central Hotel (中央饭店) was a real Nanjing hotel; the Investigation Section is said to have kept an early stronghold near it before moving to the Zhanyuan, a way-station only thinly attested. (The hotel corroborated; the detail uncorroborated.)

ch04.anchor: Emergency Law for Crimes Endangering the Republic
ch04.note: The Emergency Law for Crimes Endangering the Republic (危害民国紧急治罪法), promulgated by the Nationalist government on January 31, 1931, prescribed death for a range of acts against the state and was the chief legal instrument used against Communists; hence the interrogator's threat of the firing squad. (Corroborated.)

Haohan (浩瀚, 'the vast') is the working alias of a senior Communist the enemy is hunting; within the Party he was known for articles published under the name in The Guide Weekly (向导), the Central Committee's organ of the 1920s. His whereabouts, and who among the arrested may be his contact, are the engine of the plot.

Winter (冬) is Ling Wen's own novel, a book within the book; like Ling Wen and the other principals it is the author's invention. The novel's protagonists are fictional, set against a real historical background; its closing appendix frames the whole as an homage to the real, largely nameless Communists executed at Longhua. (The title Winter echoes the name of Ling Wen's late husband, Long Dong, 龙冬.)

The May Thirtieth Movement (五卅运动) was the wave of anti-imperialist strikes and protests that swept China after Settlement police shot Chinese demonstrators in Shanghai on May 30, 1925; it drew many, like Ling Wen and her husband, into the revolution. The Northern Expedition she goes on to mention set out from Guangzhou in 1926; the Nationalist purge of Communists began in 1927. (Corroborated.)

Tanhuang (滩簧) opera is a family of Jiangnan folk sung-drama forms in the Wu dialect, out of which grew Shanghai opera (沪剧) and its Suzhou and Wuxi cousins; the comparison casts Miss Tao's laughter as broad and theatrical. (Corroborated.)

The Louza police station (老闸捕房), at the corner of Nanking Road and Guizhou Road, was the first branch station of the Shanghai Municipal Police in the International Settlement, and a place of grim fame: on May 30, 1925, constables firing from it into a crowd that had gathered to demand the release of arrested students killed several people and touched off the May Thirtieth Movement. (Corroborated.)

Fenglin Bridge (枫林桥), in the Xujiahui district, was the site of the Nationalist garrison's prison and execution ground from the 1927 coup until about 1928—the chief place of Communist detention and death before that office passed south to Longhua. The prison van thus carries Ling Wen past the older killing-ground on the way to the newer. (Corroborated.)

ch04.anchor: make up a table of mahjong
ch04.note: Mahjong (麻将) needs four players; Miss Tao's wish for a third cellmate 'to make up a table' is the idle joke of a bored woman used to the game. (Texture.)

Malted-milk extract (麦乳精) is a sweet, nourishing milk-and-malt powder; in the early 1930s the prized versions were imported brands such as Ovaltine (阿华田) and Horlicks (好立克), luxuries a prisoner could indeed come by only 'through someone with connections.' (Corroborated.)

The cheongsam (旗袍, qipao) was the close-fitting one-piece dress that became the standard modern women's garment of Republican Shanghai; Miss Tao's, and the sapphire-blue woolen one that later hides the letter, mark her out as a woman of fashionable means. (Corroborated.)

ch04.anchor: a satin-faced quilt rolled up on a sheet patterned with mandarin ducks
ch04.note: Mandarin ducks (鸳鸯), thought to pair for life, are the standard Chinese emblem of wedded love; on Miss Tao's bedding, with the satin quilt and the drift of perfume, they are the furnishings of a kept woman. (Texture.)

ch04.anchor: her hair bobbed to the ears
ch04.note: Hair bobbed to the ears (剪发) was the mark of the emancipated 'New Woman' and of the female student or revolutionary; in these years it could itself draw official suspicion, so that Dong Huiwen's cut, 'like a schoolteacher,' is also a quiet sign of what she is. (Corroborated.)

Nanjing Road (南京路) was the great shopping street of the International Settlement, the very emblem of modern commercial Shanghai—its department stores, cinemas and crowds; You Tianxiao sets it against Longhua, the garrison and its killing-ground, to menace Dong Huiwen. (Corroborated.)

Xu Zhenya (徐枕亚, 1889–1937) wrote Jade Pear Spirit (玉梨魂, 1912), the great bestseller of the 'Mandarin Ducks and Butterflies' school of sentimental romance. That Miss Tao's idea of a famous novelist is Xu Zhenya sets her taste pointedly against Ling Wen, whose Winter belongs to the new revolutionary literature. (Corroborated.)

ch05.note: Da Hong Pao (大红袍, 'Great Red Robe') is the most storied of the Wuyi 'rock teas,' a heavily oxidized oolong grown on the cliffs of Mount Wuyi in Fujian and long counted among the most prized teas in China.

The Nineteenth Route Army (十九路军) was the Cantonese force that put up fierce resistance to the Japanese at Shanghai in the 'January 28' Incident of 1932 (一·二八, the first Battle of Shanghai); it was afterwards sent to fight Communists in Fujian. 'Commander Cai' is the army's general Cai Tingkai (蔡廷锴). (Corroborated.)

Xuanwu Lake (玄武湖) lies against the northeastern wall of Nanjing; the drive in this chapter runs beside its stretch of the great Ming-dynasty city wall, past Jiming Temple (鸡鸣寺) and out by the Shence Gate (神策门). Nanjing was the Nationalist capital and the seat of the secret-service headquarters to which You Tianxiao reports.

ch05.anchor: that round, bridge-knobbed pot of vermilion zhuni clay
ch05.note: Zhuni (朱泥, 'vermilion clay') is a prized, iron-rich red variety of the Yixing (宜兴) purple-sand (紫砂) stoneware from which China's most esteemed small teapots are made; the 'bridge-knobbed' lid names the little arched handle on top. A zhuni pot and a good rock tea mark Mu Chuan for a man of cultivated leisure. (Corroborated.)

ch05.anchor: He rinsed the cups with the first steeping
ch05.note: Mu Chuan brews in the gongfu (工夫茶) manner: a tiny pot, a first steeping poured off to rinse the cups and rouse the leaf, then repeated short infusions. The unhurried ritual is itself part of his self-presentation. (Texture.)

The Nationalist government did import quantities of German military equipment in these years, under a German advisory mission (Wetzell, then von Seeckt); but that materiel was for the army, and no record supports the garrison's being sent a German 'electric-torture apparatus.' The device belongs to the novel, hung on a real German-military backdrop. (The German equipment corroborated; the torture apparatus the novel's.)

The period of political tutelage (训政) was the stage of one-party rule the Nationalists proclaimed in October 1928: under Sun Yat-sen's three-stage scheme (military government, tutelage, then constitutional rule), the Party would exercise power on the people's behalf until they were judged ready for it. Mu Chuan's point is that under tutelage the courts, however cowed, could not simply be dispensed with. (Corroborated.)

ch05.anchor: took a bottle of chemical from a drawer
ch05.note: The line of writing brought up on the letter is invisible ink (密写): a message in a colorless fluid—here developed by a chemical reagent, elsewhere in the book by rice-water and iodine—that shows only when the paper is treated. It was a staple of underground correspondence. (Texture.)

Xujiahui (徐家汇, the old 'Siccawei/Zikawei') was a district in the southwest of the city, long the center of the Jesuit mission—cathedral, observatory, orphanage and convent. The 'box to be called for at the counter' is a poste-restante box, a classic dead-drop for the underground's mail. (Corroborated.)

ch05.anchor: Brother Fang, as though we met face to face
ch05.note: The letter's opening, 'as though we met face to face,' renders 如晤, a conventional salutation of the classical Chinese personal letter (literally 'as if seeing you'), used to an intimate or a junior; it sets the close, resolute register of the whole message. (Corroborated.)

Xiaguan (下关) was Nanjing's railway-and-wharf district on the south bank of the Yangtze; its station, opened in 1908, was the Nanjing terminus of the Shanghai–Nanjing Railway, so that a traveler up from Shanghai arrived there. (Corroborated.)

The Blue Steel Express (蓝钢快车) was the luxury express of the Shanghai–Nanjing Railway, named for its blue-painted steel carriages; introduced about 1930, it ran the route in some five and a half hours and was the fastest and costliest way between the two cities. (Corroborated.)

ch05.anchor: something more like a family law held sway
ch05.note: Family law (家法) is the private disciplinary authority a household or clan wielded over its own; here it is the metaphor for the secret service's internal code, under which 'even execution was possible.' (Texture.)

ch05.anchor: doesn't much seem to be their central special commissioner
ch05.note: A central special commissioner (中央特派员) was an agent sent down directly by the Party Central to a local body with special authority—the role the enemy is trying to fix on one of the prisoners. (Texture.)

ch05.anchor: wealthy merchants of the two Guang provinces
ch05.note: The two Guang (两广) are Guangdong and Guangxi, the two southern provinces taken together. (Texture.)
Single-line contact (单线联系) is the underground's basic security rule: each worker knows only the one comrade above and the one below, so that a captured link cannot betray the whole chain. (Texture.)

ch05.anchor: I'll send you some new trainees from the Hangzhou training class
ch05.note: The Hangzhou training class points to a real institution: the Zhejiang Provincial Police Officers' School (浙江警官学校) at Hangzhou, founded in 1928, which from 1932 became a training ground for Dai Li's Nationalist secret service. (Corroborated.)

ch05.anchor: must be the man who opened fire on Pu'enjishi Road
ch05.note: Pu'enjishi Road (普恩济世路) was a real street of the French Concession—Route John Prentice, laid out in 1926 and today Jinxian Road (进贤路)—running near the Lyceum Theatre; the bun-shop rendezvous on it is the novel's. (Corroborated.)

ch06.note: The encirclement and suppression campaigns (围剿) were the Nationalists' successive military drives from 1930 against the Communist base areas, above all the Central Soviet (中央苏区) in Jiangxi–Fujian, whose capital was Ruijin; the Communists fought them as 'counter-encirclement.' The Fourth was under way in the winter of 1932–33. In the movement's usual geography the country divided into 'Red' or Soviet areas and the 'White areas' (白区) under Nationalist rule, where the novel's underground works. (Corroborated.)

Brigade Commander Weng is Weng Zhaoyuan (翁照垣, 1892–1972), a brigade commander of the Nineteenth Route Army who took the first Japanese assault at Zhabei on the night of January 28, 1932; both the man and the Zhabei defense are historical. He is a different man from the Cantonese 'Adjutant Weng' of the earlier chapters. (Corroborated.)

The Guangzhou Uprising (广州起义, the Canton Uprising of December 11–13, 1927) was a Communist insurrection that briefly proclaimed a 'Guangzhou Commune' before being crushed with heavy loss of life — the last of the failed urban risings of 1927. (Corroborated.)

ch06.anchor: There are no miracles in nature or history
ch06.note: The lines Chen Qianyuan is translating are the opening of Lenin's Letters from Afar (远方来信), First Letter, written from Zurich in March 1917; the wording here follows the standard English of Lenin's Collected Works. The next chapter of the novel takes its title, 'A Letter from Afar,' from this same work. (Corroborated.)

After the Japanese attack on Shanghai in the 'January 28' war of 1932, the city's garrison was hurriedly fitted with air defenses; the sweeping anti-aircraft searchlights over Longhua are a lingering mark of that fighting, a year on. (Corroborated.)

ch06.anchor: no more than a hundred-odd silver dollars
ch06.note: A silver dollar (银元, the 'big money,' 大洋) was the standard silver coin of Republican China; that the pooled pockets of eleven arrested men come to only 'a hundred-odd' of them is meant to show how thin a gambling stake it makes. (Corroborated.)
The walls have ears renders 隔墙有耳 (literally 'beyond the wall there are ears')—the same warning as the English idiom, that one may be overheard anywhere. (Idiom.)

The International News Agency is Chen Qianyuan's cover: a desk translating foreign wire dispatches into Chinese, respectable work for a young man with languages. The best-known agency of the name (国际新闻社) was founded only in 1938, so the reference is generic rather than to a documented 1933 body. (Uncorroborated.)

ch07.note: In early 1933 Chiang Kai-shek directed the anti-Communist campaigns in person from Nanchang (南昌), Jiangxi; his formal Nanchang Field Headquarters (南昌行营) followed in May 1933, the forward command post for the Fourth and Fifth Encirclement Campaigns. (Corroborated.)

Xinjing (新京, 'New Capital,' today Changchun) was the capital of Manchukuo (满洲国), the puppet state Japan proclaimed in the occupied Northeast in March 1932. A merchant 'from Xinjing' in 1933 Shanghai is thus a man arriving from Japanese-held Manchuria — a loaded provenance, and part of Chen Qianli's cover. (Corroborated.)

Shanhaiguan (山海关), the pass where the Great Wall meets the sea, was stormed and taken by Japanese forces on January 1–3, 1933, opening the Defense of the Great Wall campaign (长城抗战) as Japan pushed south from Manchuria; it fixes the novel's atmosphere of national crisis. (Corroborated.)
Shen Bao (申报), founded in 1872 and published in Shanghai, was the most important Chinese-language newspaper of the Republican era. (Corroborated.)

Khabarovsk (伯力), in the Soviet Far East, places Chen Qianli's three years of training in the USSR — the Soviet and Comintern schooling that stood behind many senior Chinese Communist operatives of the period; his long way out (Khabarovsk to Vladivostok, then by sea) follows a real clandestine route. The school itself is the novel's; the geography is real.

The Outpost (前哨) was the organ of the League of Left-Wing Writers; its first issue (April 1931), edited by Lu Xun (鲁迅) and Feng Xuefeng (冯雪峰), was a memorial number for the writers murdered at Longhua weeks before. This stretch of North Sichuan Road (北四川路) in Hongkou was the heart of the leftist literary world; Chen Geng (陈赓), the Red Army commander named here, really did meet Lu Xun secretly in Shanghai in 1932. (Corroborated.)

The Yihong Garden (扆虹园), a Cantonese garden-mansion in the North Sichuan Road quarter, was visited more than once by Sun Yat-sen (孙中山, 'Mr. Sun') — in 1912–13 Guangdong native-place associations fêted him there. (Corroborated.)

The Left League is the League of Left-Wing Writers (左联), founded in Shanghai in 1930; five of its young members were among the Communists shot at Longhua in February 1931 whom the novel commemorates. (Corroborated.)
The Nanchang Uprising (南昌起义) of August 1, 1927 was the Communists' first armed revolt against the Nationalists, afterwards marked as the founding day of the Red Army. (Corroborated.)

The German Hospital (德国医院) was the real Paulun Hospital (宝隆医院), founded in 1900 by the German physician Erich Paulun and tied to what became Tongji University's medical school; it stood in the Settlement, and its later descendant is Shanghai's Changzheng Hospital. (Corroborated.)

A surety bond (铺保, pubao) was a real institution of Republican Shanghai: a shop, pledging its name and chop, stood as guarantor for a third party — a tenant, an employee, or a prisoner seeking bail — and bore joint liability if that party defaulted. Here the underground turns the custom to its own use, springing arrested comrades on a shopkeeper’s guarantee. (Corroborated.)

ch07.anchor: the mouth of the Wusong River
ch07.note: The mouth of the Wusong River (吴淞口, Woosung), where the Huangpu joins the Yangtze, was the outer anchorage of the port of Shanghai; incoming steamers lay there to take on a river pilot and be boarded by the Settlement's foreign police before proceeding up to the city wharves. (Corroborated.)

ch07.anchor: the smell of salted fish and cured meats
ch07.note: Against the New Year, Shanghai households hang out salted fish and cured meats (腊味) to dry—the winter provisioning that, with firecrackers and the settling of debts, marks the approach of the festival. (Texture.)

The Post Office building Chen Qianli circles is the Shanghai General Post Office (上海邮政总局), the landmark at the north end of the Sichuan Road Bridge over Suzhou Creek, built in 1922–24 with a columned façade and a Baroque clock tower—then reckoned the finest post office in the Far East. (Corroborated.)

ch07.anchor: the Shuimo Bookshop and the Xinken Bookshop in Gongyi Lane
ch07.note: The Shuimo Bookshop (水沫书店) and Xinken Bookshop (辛垦书店) in Gongyi Lane (公益坊) were real: Gongyi Lane, off North Sichuan Road in Hongkou, was a nest of small leftist and modernist presses, and the Shuimo Bookshop was founded in 1928 by the writers Shi Zhecun (施蛰存), Dai Wangshu (戴望舒) and Liu Na'ou (刘呐鸥). This was the ground of the leftist literary world the novel keeps returning to. (Corroborated.)

ch07.anchor: straight on to Shengmuyuan Road next to it
ch07.note: Shengmuyuan Road (圣母院路, 'Convent Road,' the French Concession's Route des Sœurs, today Ruijin Yi Road) was named for the Xujiahui convent; Old Fang's escape runs from Pu'enjishi Road through the through-lanes to it. (Corroborated.)

ch07.anchor: cloth banners calling for a boycott of Japanese goods
ch07.note: The banners call for a boycott of Japanese goods (抵制日货): the anti-Japanese economic movement that surged after the Mukden Incident of 1931 and the January 28 war, when patriotic associations pressed shops to drop Japanese wares—so effective that Japanese imports to Shanghai for a time collapsed. (Corroborated.)

ch07.anchor: in July of the eighteenth year of the Republic
ch07.note: Dates are here reckoned by the Republican calendar (民国纪年), which counts 1912 as year one; the eighteenth year of the Republic is thus 1929 (1911 + 18). (Corroborated.)

ch07.anchor: the Great Revolution had been in ruins two years
ch07.note: The Great Revolution (大革命, also 国民革命) is the standard name for the years 1924–27 of the Nationalist–Communist alliance and the Northern Expedition, which collapsed in the 1927 split and purge; 'in ruins two years' places Yi Junnian's transfer to Shanghai in 1929. (Corroborated.)

ch07.anchor: was making ready a modern-style ceremony
ch07.note: A modern-style ceremony renders 文明结婚, the 'civilized wedding' that spread in Republican cities—a reformed, partly Westernized rite, with an officiant and vows, that replaced the traditional 'six rites.' (Corroborated.)

Shikumen (石库门, 'stone-framed gate') are the terraced lane-houses that were the characteristic dwelling of old Shanghai, built in long rows behind a stone doorway, each with its small courtyard-well (天井) and a flat rooftop drying-terrace (晒台). Because the rows abut roof to roof, they make the over-the-roofs escape Chen Qianli takes. (Corroborated.)

Shanghai's electric trams (电车) ran from 1908, worked in the Settlement and the French Concession by rival companies; they were the cheap, ubiquitous public transport of the modern city. (Corroborated.)

ch08.note: The Grand Theatre (大光明大戏院), on today's West Nanjing Road, was Shanghai's most celebrated cinema; the László Hudec rebuild that made it an Art Deco landmark was completed in mid-1933, just as this chapter is set. (Corroborated.)

Marlene Dietrich (玛琳·黛德丽, 1901–1992), the German-American film star, had lately played 'Shanghai Lily' in Shanghai Express (1932); her face on a Shanghai cinema hoarding in 1933 is exactly of its moment. (Corroborated.)

Turandot, Puccini's last opera (premiered posthumously in 1926), is set in a legendary Peking whose princess beheads the suitors who fail her riddles; the poster's line condenses the opera's blood-soaked opening — the executioner's chorus, 'Gira la cote' ('turn the grindstone') — rather than quoting it. The touring San Carlo company was real, though a 1933 Carlton staging is not separately documented. (The opera corroborated; the Shanghai performance uncorroborated.)

As the Japanese advanced in early 1933, the Palace Museum in Beiping (北平, as Beijing was then called) began evacuating its treasures south; the first crates left the Forbidden City on the night of February 5–6, 1933, and the removal filled the newspapers exactly as the chapter describes. (Corroborated.)

ch08.anchor: the Four Banks' Savings Society building
ch08.note: The tower going up across from the racecourse is the Park Hotel (国际饭店), developed by the Joint Savings Society of four banks (四行储蓄会) to a design by László Hudec and completed in 1934; at twenty-two storeys it was the tallest building in Asia for nearly thirty years. (Corroborated.)

ch08.anchor: the Four Masters of the Ming
ch08.note: The Four Masters of the Ming (明四家) are Shen Zhou, Wen Zhengming, Tang Yin and Qiu Ying (仇英); Qiu Ying alone was a professional artisan-painter, a master of meticulous brushwork whose much-prized manner made him one of the most heavily forged names in Chinese painting — apt for a tale of a fake. (Corroborated.)
The racecourse is the great oval of the Shanghai Race Club, a center of foreign social life; its grounds are today People's Square and People's Park. (Corroborated.)
The Grand Champagne (大香槟) was the Race Club's celebrated sweepstakes lottery, drawn on the big races; here the split ticket serves the plot as a recognition token. (Corroborated.)
The Xiaolin Guangji (笑林广记, 'Expanded Forest of Laughter') is the best-known of the classical Chinese joke-books, compiled in the Qing dynasty. (Corroborated.)

Morriss (马立斯) renders the name of the British Morriss family, proprietors of the North-China Daily News; the transliteration is well attested in old Shanghai, though the particular building named here, by the racecourse, is not separately documented. (The name corroborated; the building uncorroborated.)

ch08.anchor: then turned left into Park Road
ch08.note: Park Road (派克路, today Huanghe Road), a short street along the eastern edge of the racecourse, ran past the Carlton Theatre where the Turandot of this chapter plays; it lay in the bright amusement quarter north of the race club. (Corroborated.)

The Guangyi Book Company (广益书局) was a Shanghai commercial publisher (from 1900) known for cheap popular editions of vernacular fiction and reference works such as this joke-book; a specific Guangyi printing of the Xiaolin Guangji is likely but not separately attested. (The publisher corroborated; this edition uncorroborated.)

ch08.anchor: A charitable donation of one national dollar is deducted
ch08.note: The ticket's line reflects the Race Club's practice of skimming a fixed charity levy from every Grand Champagne stake; a national dollar (国币) was one silver yuan, the standard unit of the Nationalist currency before the paper fabi of 1935. (Corroborated.)
Neon advertising signs (霓虹灯) were a new marvel of Shanghai's nightscape—the first had appeared on Nanjing Road in 1926—and by 1933 traced the skyline of the modern city. (Corroborated.)

The plane trees whose leaves blow here (popularly 法国梧桐, 'French wutong,' from the French concession's plantings of the 1880s) were the London planes that became, and remain, the emblematic street tree of old Shanghai. (Corroborated.)

ch09.note: The April Twelfth massacre (四一二, 1927) was Chiang Kai-shek’s sudden purge of his Communist allies in Shanghai on April 12, 1927, carried out with Green Gang gunmen against the workers’ pickets and unions. It shattered the first Nationalist–Communist united front and drove the Party into the deep-cover underground this novel depicts; casualty counts vary, and the wider ‘White Terror’ toll is estimated in the thousands and beyond. (Corroborated; exact figures are estimates.)

Wu Sibao (吴四宝) is the name of a real Shanghai figure (c. 1904–1942): a racecourse groom who became a chauffeur, rose through the Green Gang, and under the Japanese occupation led the armed unit of the collaborationist ‘No. 76’ secret service. The novel plants him here as a minor tenant, his groom-to-driver rise matching the record; that he was Ling Wen’s neighbor is the novel’s own touch. (The man corroborated; his role here the novel’s invention.)

ch09.anchor: A rabbit doesn't eat the grass by its own burrow
ch09.note: A Chinese proverb, 兔子不吃窝边草 — literally ‘a rabbit does not eat the grass beside its own burrow’ — meaning a rogue spares those closest to home. The point is that the racecourse tough keeps on civil terms with his own neighbors. (Idiom.)

A second landlord (二房东) is a sub-lessor who leases a whole house and lets its rooms on at a profit — a stock figure of crowded Shanghai. It is Ling Wen’s cover: the tenancy, taken in her late husband’s name, both houses her and, because a lease could not be revoked without cause, cannot easily be taken from her.

ch09.anchor: we've paid a bitter price for that before
ch09.note: The ‘bitter price’ alludes to the Party’s own real purges of 1930–31: the hunt for a supposed Nationalist network, the ‘AB Corps’ (AB团), and the Futian Incident of December 1930, in which thousands of Red Army personnel were arrested on coerced evidence and hundreds executed — a catastrophe Mao himself later acknowledged as a mistake. Yi Junnian’s caution against branding comrades as moles has this history behind it. (Corroborated; death tolls are estimates.)

Hongkou Park (虹口公园) was the largest public park of foreign Shanghai, in the Hongkou district; today it is Lu Xun Park (鲁迅公园). It was a real, popular place to stroll and be photographed — and, less than a year before this scene, the site of the April 29, 1932 bombing by the Korean patriot Yun Bong-gil. (Corroborated.)

The song is Tumbalalaika, a traditional Yiddish folk love-song of riddles, its refrain playing on the name of the balalaika, the Russian triangular-bodied lute the busker holds. Both song and instrument are real; the tune has nineteenth-century Eastern-European folk roots, and an Ashkenazi (Russian-Jewish) busker in 1930s Shanghai is historically plausible, that community predating the later refugee wave. (Corroborated.)

The Leica, made by Ernst Leitz of Wetzlar, was the pioneering 35mm miniature camera; the rangefinder Leica II appeared in 1932, so a Leica is exactly of this moment as a prestige, cutting-edge instrument. (Corroborated.)

ch09.anchor: A vase of flowers was the safe signal
ch09.note: A prearranged safe signal—here a vase of flowers in the window (elsewhere a lit lamp, a drawn curtain)—told an approaching comrade that the house was not being watched; its absence meant danger. Such all-clear signs were standard underground tradecraft. (Texture.)

ch09.anchor: hand her a cigarette or a wax pellet
ch09.note: A wax pellet (蜡丸) is a written message rolled tight and sealed in a ball of wax—waterproof, easily hidden or swallowed, and destroyed by dropping it in water; the method of carrying secret dispatches is an old one, attested since the Song dynasty. (Corroborated.)

ch09.anchor: We mustn't play the exploiting class
ch09.note: The exploiting class (剥削阶级) is the Marxist category of those who live off others' labor—here the landlords; Ling Wen's refusal to raise the rent is a point of Communist principle kept up even inside her cover as a sub-letting landlady. (Texture.)

The sources Yi Junnian taps—the municipal Party headquarters (市党部, the Nationalists' Shanghai party organ), the police department, the Municipal Police—are the very bodies hunting the Communists; that his network reaches inside them all is what makes him so valuable, and, to the reader, so opaque. (Texture.)

ch10.note: The Zhonghui Bank (中汇银行), rendered here as the ‘Zhonghui Trust Bank,’ was real: founded in 1929 by the Green Gang boss Du Yuesheng, it ran a genuine trust department and safe-deposit vault, so a rented box there is authentic to the setting. (Corroborated; the ‘Trust Bank’ name follows the novel’s 信托银行.)

Guanshengyuan (冠生园) was a famous Shanghai food-and-confectionery company, founded in 1915 by Xian Guansheng and celebrated for its pastries and mooncakes; a well-known brand by 1933, its pastry box completes Ling Wen’s wealthy-wife disguise. (Corroborated.)

Here the source drops into stiff classical business-letter Chinese — 径启者 (‘I beg to state’), 大鉴, 为荷 — a formulaic epistolary register quite unlike the surrounding prose. The translation keeps that starched formality to mark the shift; the letter itself is a coded notice about a safe-deposit box.
The Rentai Bank Company (仁泰银公司), Lin Shi’s cover employer, is a realistic native-bank name but is not attested in the record and appears to be the novel’s invention. (Uncorroborated.)

Cut off from their leadership, the freed comrades form a provisional Party branch (临时党支部), improvising the Party’s cell structure so as to keep discipline and act together. It is also what licenses their alarming, self-appointed interrogation of Lin Shi.

Shanghai lane addresses stack their units: a named compound of terraced houses (a fang 坊 or li 里—here 'Sancheng Fang, Tongfu Li'), a numbered lane (long 弄) within it, and a house number. The layered address is itself a small map of the lane-house city. (Texture.)

ch10.anchor: the archway house at the lane mouth
ch10.note: The archway house (过街楼) is a room built out over the mouth of a lane, spanning the entrance passage; the clinic occupies one such upper room. (Texture.)

A Western-Medicine Clinic (西医诊所) advertised modern, foreign-trained scientific medicine, as against a practitioner of Chinese medicine; the distinction, and the doctor's German-hospital training, place Qin Chuan'an among the Westernized professional class. (Texture.)

ch10.anchor: he could still be carrying his seal on him
ch10.note: A seal (图章/私章), a small stamp cut with one's name, served as a personal signature on Chinese documents and letters; Tian Fei's point is that the letter is validated with such a seal, which an ordinary bank clerk would hardly carry through arrest and prison. (Texture.)
Kites with cut strings (断线的风筝) is the idiom for people or things adrift and past all control—here the comrades cut off from the organization. (Idiom.)

A pillar-box is the free-standing cylindrical street letter-box of the British postal tradition, as used by the Settlement and Concession posts; Qin Chuan'an means to drop the letter into it unobserved. (Texture.)

ch11.anchor: A muddy Winter Solstice, a clear New Year
ch11.note: A Jiangnan weather proverb, 邋遢冬至清爽年: overcast, muddy weather at the Winter Solstice is taken to foretell a fine, clear New Year (and the reverse). It is folk lore, not meteorology. (Corroborated as a traditional saying.)

Jing’an Temple (静安寺), the ancient Buddhist temple on Bubbling Well Road (today Nanjing West Road), gave its name to the surrounding district. The custom of vying to burn the ‘first incense’ (头香) at the New Year, mentioned just below, is a real and famous feature of the place. (Corroborated.)

‘Cement’ here renders 水门汀, the Shanghainese transliteration of the English word (concrete); a 水门汀 house is a cement or reinforced-concrete building, the modern, desirable sort in 1930s Shanghai. (Corroborated.)
Zhaojiabang (肇嘉浜) was a real Shanghai creek, its banks crowded with wharves and yards in the 1930s; it was filled in during 1954–56 to make Zhaojiabang Road. (Corroborated.)

Route Massenet (马斯南路), the recognition-signal address, was a real French Concession street named for the composer Jules Massenet; today it is Sinan Road (思南路), the modern name chosen partly to echo the old one in Shanghainese. (Corroborated.)

The streets Wei Dafu reels off are all real roads of the old western Concessions: Avenue Haig (海格路; today Huashan Road), Shanzhong Road (善钟路, the one Concession road named for a Chinese, the land magnate Tao Shanzhong; today Changshu Road), and Zhaozhujiao Road (赵主教路, Route Monseigneur Maresca, for the Catholic bishop of Nanjing; today Wuyuan Road). (Corroborated.)

Red China (红色中华) was the real newspaper of the Chinese Soviet Republic’s central government, first published at Ruijin on December 11, 1931; the Third Counter-Encirclement Campaign whose victory it reports was the Red Army’s defeat, in the autumn of 1931, of the Nationalists’ third ‘encirclement and suppression’ drive against the Central Soviet. To keep a copy in the White area was dangerous in itself. (Corroborated.)
An Old Bolshevik is a veteran who joined the Party in its earliest years; applied to Old Yi, it marks his seniority and long standing in the revolution.

The Tiangu Estate (田谷邨) is a new-style lane compound on the real, exclusive Yuyuan Road; the specific name is not attested (it echoes the actual 愚谷邨, Yugu Cun, on that street), though the setting and building type are true to the period. (The street corroborated; this estate uncorroborated.)

ch11.anchor: work the streets in that foreign suit of his
ch11.note: Wei Dafu’s wish to work in a foreign suit rather than his padded gown (棉袍) is a matter of class signaling: by the 1930s a Western suit read as modern, moneyed and businesslike, and the long Chinese gown as old-fashioned, so a street salesman felt that in a suit he could talk a client round with, as he puts it, ‘a full chest.’ (Texture.)

The exchange about which end of the street has a T-junction is a recognition signal (对暗号), the underground’s challenge-and-countersign: a fixed, innocuous-sounding question with a set reply, by which two comrades who have never met confirm each other. By the rules it is used only when a comrade from higher up comes to make contact, which is why Wei Dafu, whose only uplines have been Old Fang and Yi Junnian, has all but forgotten it. (Texture.)

ch11.anchor: on the border between the Settlement and the Chinese city
ch11.note: Shanghai was divided among jurisdictions that did not cooperate — the International Settlement, the French Concession, and the Chinese-administered city and county, each with its own police, none free to pursue a suspect across the line. A safe house set on the border, with exits into two of them, let the underground slip from one force’s reach into another’s; this is the tradecraft advantage Chen Qianli asks for. (Texture.)

ch12.note: Tilanqiao Prison (提篮桥监狱), the ‘Ward Road Gaol,’ was built by the International Settlement authorities in Hongkou and opened in 1903; long one of the largest prisons in the Far East — it was nicknamed ‘the Far East’s No. 1 prison’ — it still stands. Chen Qianli passes its gate in the foreign-flavored streets north of Suzhou Creek. (Corroborated.)

By the early 1930s the lanes of Hongkou around Tilanqiao were already a foreign working-class quarter — Russian émigrés who had fled the 1917 Revolution, and Russian and Baghdadi Jews among others — with institutions such as the Ohel Moshe Synagogue (its building of 1927) nearby. This earlier settlement predates, and is distinct from, the crowded refugee ‘ghetto’ the Japanese would impose on the same district in 1943 for Jews who fled Nazi Europe after 1938; the old man in the orange skullcap belongs to the older layer. (Corroborated.)

The tingzijian (亭子间) is the small, cheap back room over the kitchen landing of a Shanghai lane house — north-facing, low and cramped, the least desirable room to let, and so the classic lodging of the poor left-wing writers of 1930s Shanghai, the ‘tingzijian writers’ (亭子间文人). (Corroborated.)

Ye Tao (叶桃), here named for the first time, is Ye Qinian’s daughter and Chen Qianli’s love; her death — which Chen lays at her father’s door, and which the enemy means to fasten on Chen — is the buried wound that drives him, and, on the other side, feeds Ye Qinian’s hatred. Like the novel’s other principals she is the author’s invention. (Fiction.)

Nekrasov is the Russian poet Nikolai Nekrasov (1821–1877). The line the brothers keep as a private countersign — ‘They say the storm is coming, and I cannot help but smile’ — adapts a couplet from his early poem The Storm (Burya); but that poem is a light love lyric, not a political one — a young man, after a thunderstorm spoils a garden tryst, ever after smiles rather than frowns to hear a storm coming. The novel re-weaponizes its storm-and-smile image, and the Chinese ‘they say…is coming’ freely paraphrases the original. (The poem and the line are corroborated; the revolutionary coloring is the novel’s.)

Shaoshan (少山) was a real cover name of Zhou Enlai (周恩来) in the Shanghai underground — the name under which, in the 1932 ‘Wu Hao Incident,’ a lawyer publicly rebutted a forged notice of his defection. Sending Chen Qianli to the USSR through ‘Comrade Shaoshan’ borrows the historical alias; strictly, Zhou had already left Shanghai for the Central Soviet by late 1931, so the handler of this early-1933 scene is a compressed, literary use of the name. (The alias is corroborated as Zhou’s; the scene is the novel’s.)

Duoyunxuan (朵云轩), founded in Shanghai in 1900, was a celebrated studio for fine paper, fans and painting supplies, famous for decorated letter-paper printed by woodblock watermark. That the poem is written on a sheet printed with a spray of peach blossom is a private stroke: 桃, táo, ‘peach,’ is the given name of Ye Tao (叶桃). (The studio is corroborated; the peach-blossom pun is the novel’s.)

The Esperanto study group and Teacher Ye’s dictum that ‘the world of the future will have but one language’ place him in a real milieu: Chinese anarchists were among the earliest champions of Esperanto, which they promoted as a coming universal tongue that would dissolve nation and state. Ye Qinian’s early anarchism, and his scorn for ‘those Russian books,’ belong to that world. (Corroborated.)

ch12.anchor: the rice-water for the secret writing
ch12.note: The rice-water (米浆水) is invisible ink: a message written in rice-starch water dries unseen and is brought out by brushing the paper with tincture of iodine, which turns the starch strokes blue-black. Cheap and untraceable, it was a genuine and much-used method of the Communist underground’s clandestine correspondence. (Corroborated.)

Chengzhong Middle School (澄衷中学) was a real Hongkou school, founded about 1900 by the Ningbo merchant Ye Chengzhong (叶澄衷, 1840–1899) as the first influential Chinese-run modern school in Shanghai; Cai Yuanpei served as its first dean of studies, and Hu Shi was among its early pupils. It added a middle-school course and took the name Chengzhong Middle School in 1928, and survives today in Hongkou as Shanghai Chengzhong Senior High School. (Corroborated.)

The Xiahai Temple (下海庙) is a real Hongkou temple, founded in the Qianlong reign (1736–95) by local boatmen and fishermen to worship the sea deities and later turned into a Buddhist nunnery; it is named for the Xiahai Pu (下海浦), a creek of the old Hongkou waterfront. Burned in the Japanese shelling early in the war and afterward rebuilt, it stands today at the corner of Kunming and Haimen Roads. (The temple is corroborated; the ‘Maohai Road’ corner is the novel’s own geography.)

ch12.anchor: The training school had once been the manor of some old aristocrat
ch12.note: Chen Qianli’s three years at a training school in the Soviet Union reflect a real practice: the Comintern trained Chinese Communist cadres in Moscow at the Communist University of the Toilers of the East (from 1921), Sun Yat-sen University (1925–30), and the elite International Lenin School (from 1926), whose core course ran three years. The novel leaves the school unnamed; the ‘old aristocrat’s manor’ and the ‘Siberian forest’ beyond the wire are atmosphere, not a real campus, all three schools being in or near Moscow. (Soviet cadre-training corroborated; this particular school the novel’s own.)

ch12.anchor: Give them one striking feature first
ch12.note: Putting on ‘one striking feature’ — here a conspicuous russet hat and scarf, swapped in a crowd for a plain gray homburg — is real tradecraft: a tail fixes on the memorable detail, so shedding it effectively erases the man the pursuer was told to follow. (Texture.)

Letters from Afar (远方来信) is Lenin’s series of five letters written from Zurich in March 1917, on the eve of his return to Russia after the February Revolution; only the first was published at the time. The manuscript Chen Qianyuan is translating, headed ‘First Letter: The First Stage of the First Revolution,’ is that actual first letter, whose title is exactly ‘The First Stage of the First Revolution’; it gives this chapter its Chinese title, 远方来信. (Corroborated.)
Tangyuan (汤圆) are boiled glutinous-rice balls, often filled with sweet sesame or bean paste, eaten at New Year and the Lantern Festival; their roundness stands for family reunion. (Corroborated.)

ch13.anchor: the Eve of the Abolished Calendar
ch13.note: From 1929 the Nanjing government pressed the ‘National Calendar’ (国历, the Gregorian) on the country and set out to abolish the lunar year, banning its holiday, its New Year calls and its firecrackers; the old calendar was officially styled the ‘abolished calendar’ (废历), so that lunar New Year’s Eve became the Eve of the Abolished Calendar. As the chapter shows, the public almost wholly ignored the ban and kept the old year as before. (Corroborated.)

The Cathay Hotel (华懋饭店), Victor Sassoon’s Art Deco landmark on the Bund (part of Sassoon House, opened 1929, today the north building of the Peace Hotel), gives the chapter its title and its stage: the green pyramidal roof, the octagonal lobby rotunda under its colored-glass dome, and the revolving door at the Bund entrance are all real. Ye Qinian’s choosing to lodge ‘in Sassoon’s own house, in the house of the imperialists’ is pointed. (Corroborated.)

The sneezing foreigner in the star-patterned sweater is George Bernard Shaw. On his round-the-world cruise Shaw reached Shanghai on February 17, 1933, where in a few hours he met Soong Ching-ling, Cai Yuanpei and Lu Xun; days before, at the University of Hong Kong (February 11–12), he had scandalized the colonial authorities by urging the students to revolution — ‘if you are not a red revolutionist at twenty…’ The mobbing reporters and the world cruise are real; the sneeze and the sweater are the novel’s color. (Corroborated.)
The seventy-two transformations are the shape-shifting powers of the Monkey King, Sun Wukong, in the classic novel Journey to the West — a byword for a trickster who can take any form. (Allusion.)

The famous saying Shaw is said to have ‘garbled’ is the old epigram that one who is not a radical in youth has no heart, but one still radical in age has no head — commonly credited to Guizot or Clemenceau, and, in an 1872 form, to the jurist Anselme Batbie citing Burke; Ye Qinian’s giving it to ‘a judge’ fits the Batbie strand. Its author is genuinely disputed. (The saying is corroborated; the attribution is not settled.)

ch13.anchor: there's a crab on your belly
ch13.note: The band is playing a foreign dance tune the novel calls ‘I Belong to Your Heart,’ which Chinese ears are said to have misheard as 肚皮上有一只蟹, ‘there’s a crab on your belly.’ The homophonic joke has the flavor of old-Shanghai lore, but it is untraceable in the reliable record, and no dance tune of exactly that title fixes it to 1933; treat it as a likely apocryphal grace-note. (Uncorroborated.)

Mr. Lifu is Chen Lifu (陈立夫, 1900–2001), who with his brother Chen Guofu led the Kuomintang’s ‘CC Clique’; as head of the Central Organization Department he stood over the Party Affairs Investigation Section, the KMT’s political-intelligence organ, and was in 1933 the controlling figure of its secret work — hence the man for Ye Qinian to ‘put in a word’ with. (Corroborated.)

Bogu — Bo Gu — was the alias of Qin Bangxian (秦邦宪, 1907–1946), de facto head of the Chinese Communists’ Provisional Central in Shanghai. Ye Qinian’s inference is historically exact: on a decision of January 13, 1933 the Provisional Central quit the dangerous Shanghai underground for the Central Soviet, and Bo Gu and his colleagues reached Ruijin by late January 1933 — just as a Red China article signed ‘Bogu’ would suggest. (Corroborated.)

ch13.anchor: The Bund is just as it was
ch13.note: The Bund (外滩) is the mile-long riverfront boulevard along the Huangpu in the International Settlement, from the 1860s the banking and commercial heart of Shanghai and, by the 1930s, of East Asia — a row of monumental foreign banks, trading houses and hotels, the Cathay among them. It was the emblem of colonial, cosmopolitan Shanghai; Ye Qinian gazes down on it from Sassoon’s hotel. (Corroborated.)

ch13.anchor: he did the occasional tea dance himself
ch13.note: A tea dance (茶舞, from the French thé dansant) was a fashionable late-afternoon social dance of the 1920s and 1930s; in Shanghai it was a fixture of elite hotel and cabaret life, the Cathay hosting the celebrated Sassoon tea dance. That You Tianxiao ‘did the occasional tea dance’ marks him for the modern, moneyed, Westernized world. (Corroborated.)

ch14.note: The workers’ pickets (工人纠察队) were the armed labor militia of the Communist-led Shanghai workers’ uprisings that seized the Chinese city as the Northern Expedition neared in early 1927, above all the third uprising of March 21, 1927. Cui Wentai’s rise through the strikes and the pickets, and his shelter by Old Fang, set his whole history against these events. (Corroborated.)

The Twenty-Sixth Army (二十六军) of the National Revolutionary Army, under Zhou Fengqi and the overall command of Bai Chongxi, carried out the Shanghai side of Chiang Kai-shek’s April Twelfth coup of 1927: on April 12–13 it tricked the workers’ pickets into surrendering their arms and then machine-gunned the protesting crowd on Baoshan Road, seizing and shooting the pickets’ leaders. The novel’s naming of the 26th Army is historically exact. (Corroborated.)

The great floods of the twentieth year of the Republic are the catastrophic Central China floods of 1931, among the deadliest disasters of the twentieth century, which spread famine and epidemic disease, cholera among them; death-toll estimates diverge sharply, from around 145,000 in Chinese sources to some 3.7–4 million in Western ones. (Corroborated; the toll is estimated within a wide range.)

The New Year’s Eve table is set with Shanghai home-style (本帮) classics: zaobodou (糟钵斗), assorted pork offal stewed in fermented-glutinous-rice sauce; oil-seared shrimp (油爆虾); yanduxian (腌笃鲜), a soup of salt pork and fresh pork simmered with bamboo shoots; and the five-kernel New Year cake (年糕), whose name puns on 年年高, ‘higher year after year.’ (Corroborated.)

Shaoxing wine (绍兴酒) is a huangjiu or ‘yellow wine,’ a fermented (not distilled) rice wine from Shaoxing in Zhejiang, amber and mellow and far milder than grain spirit; the classic banquet and festival drink of the Jiangnan region, served warmed, which is why a crock of it is brought to the New Year’s Eve table. (Corroborated.)

The Mauser pistol is the German Mauser C96, known in China as the 盒子炮 (‘box cannon’) or 驳壳枪 for its wooden holster-stock — a bulky, long-barreled semi-automatic recognizable by the box magazine set before the trigger. Because the arms embargoes of the 1920s restricted rifles but not pistols, it poured into China by the hundreds of thousands and became the favored sidearm of soldiers, gangsters and revolutionaries alike. (Corroborated.)

ch14.anchor: the Fourth Company of the Fifteenth Bao in Fengxian
ch14.note: A bao (保) was a unit of the baojia, the old household-registration and local-defense system in which about a hundred households made a bao under a headman, used for policing, conscription and mutual surveillance; Fengxian (奉贤) is the marshy coastal county south of Shanghai. The Nationalists revived the baojia in full, as an anti-Communist control apparatus, only from 1932, so a formally numbered bao belongs to the system as it was being systematized around this time. (Corroborated; the numbered-bao apparatus is a c.1932 development.)

ch15.note: The storming of the Soviet consulate in Guangzhou is real: on December 13, 1927, retaking the city from the Communist ‘Canton Commune,’ Nationalist and allied forces raided the Soviet consulate-general and shot five of its staff, along with Chinese employees, and Nationalist China broke off relations with the USSR soon after. Whether Long Dong really died there is the novel’s question, not history’s. (The raid and the killings are corroborated.)

ch15.anchor: A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains
ch15.note: A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains (千里江山图) is a real painting, and the novel’s title: a blue-green landscape handscroll on silk, about 51.5 cm high and 11.9 meters long, painted in 1113 by Wang Ximeng (王希孟), a pupil of the Song emperor Huizong, at the age of eighteen. It is his only surviving work and one of the most celebrated of all Chinese paintings, held today in the Palace Museum, Beijing. Here its name is the underground’s passphrase, and the mission is named for it — a thousand li of courier line, and a thousand li of the rivers and mountains of China. (Corroborated.)

The August 7th Conference (八七会议), an emergency meeting of the Communist Party’s Central Committee held secretly at Hankou on August 7, 1927, met in the wreckage of the First United Front after Chiang Kai-shek’s April purge. It repudiated Chen Duxiu’s ‘right opportunism,’ set the general line of land revolution and armed resistance to the Nationalists, and raised Qu Qiubai to the leadership; it was here that Mao Zedong pressed the view that political power grows from the barrel of a gun. (Corroborated.)

Jianren (简任) was the second-highest of the four grades of the Nationalist civil service (特任, 简任, 荐任, 委任), just below the ministerial 特任 appointments. The point is that the head of the Party Affairs Investigation Section, though only a middling official on paper, wielded power far beyond his nominal rank. (Corroborated.)

The Party’s clandestine courier lines (交通线) from Shanghai to the base areas were real. From 1930 the Central Liaison Bureau opened lines out of Shanghai; the enduring one, the famous ‘Central Red Route,’ ran Shanghai–Hong Kong–Shantou–Dabu–Ruijin and carried documents, funds, supplies and more than two hundred cadres (Zhou Enlai among them) into the blockaded Central Soviet until the eve of the Long March in 1934. Standard Party histories count three main lines (the Yangtze, Northern and Southern); the novel’s ‘four’ is its own figure, perhaps counting a secondary branch. (The lines are corroborated; the count of four is the novel’s.)

The Canton–Hong Kong Strike (省港大罢工) was the great general strike and anti-British boycott of 1925–26, launched in solidarity with Shanghai’s May Thirtieth Movement and inflamed by the Shakee (Shaji) shooting of June 23, 1925, when Anglo-French troops fired on demonstrators in Guangzhou. Lasting some sixteen months and drawing on the order of a quarter-million strikers, it is often called the longest strike in labor history, and the Communists were deeply involved in it. (Corroborated.)

ch15.anchor: glutinous eight-treasure rice with sweet red-bean paste
ch15.note: Eight-treasure rice (八宝饭) is a sweet steamed dessert of glutinous rice built around red-bean paste and studded with ‘eight treasures’ — dates, candied fruit, lotus seeds, melon-seed kernels and the like; a festive Jiangnan and Shanghai New Year dish, its round shape standing for reunion and ‘eight’ being a lucky number that sounds like the word for prospering. (Corroborated.)

ch16.note: The marten-paw fur (诱爪仁) — sewn, the novel says, from the tiny strips of skin below a marten’s claws, so that one robe might cost hundreds of animals — dramatizes a real practice of Chinese furriery, in which a garment is pieced from small prime parts (back, legs, paws) of many pelts. But this particular ‘under-the-claw’ category, and its extravagant claims, are not attested outside the novel and look to be its own embellishment. (The pieced-fur practice is corroborated; this specific fur is uncorroborated.)

The ABC of Communism (共产主义ABC) is a real book: Nikolai Bukharin and Yevgeni Preobrazhensky’s popular 1919 exposition of the Bolshevik party program, widely read in Chinese translation as an introduction to Communism in the 1920s. Letters from Afar is Lenin’s 1917 work (see the note at the earlier chapter that quotes it). To Ye Qinian these are the books that ‘turned’ the young Chen Qianli. (Corroborated.)

ch16.anchor: Tianjin Road was the street of the banks
ch16.note: Tianjin Road (天津路), in the old International Settlement just north of Nanjing Road, was a real hub of banks and native banks — part of the northern money market — and is commonly remembered as one of Shanghai’s ‘bank streets.’ (Corroborated.)

A native bank (钱庄, qianzhuang) was a traditional Chinese private banking house, the indigenous forerunner of the modern bank: it began in money-changing and grew into deposits, loans and remittance, running on personal credit and native-place ties and issuing its own money orders. In Republican Shanghai the native banks worked alongside the foreign and modern Chinese banks; the novel’s distinction between the 钱庄 and the modern 银行 is exactly right. (Corroborated.)

‘Big yellow croakers’ (大黄鱼) was old-Shanghai slang for gold bars: a ten-tael bar was a ‘big yellow croaker,’ a one-tael bar a ‘little yellow croaker’ (小黄鱼), ten little to one big, the names taken from the gold color and the rough fish shape. A ten-tael bar ran to roughly 310–373 grams, depending on the tael standard in use. Cui Wentai’s ‘five big yellow croakers’ are the five gold bars. (Corroborated.)

Seward Road (熙华德路), in Hongkou, was a real Settlement street built in 1864 and named for an American consul; in the 1943 wholesale renaming of foreign-named streets it became Changzhi Road (长治路), which it remains. (Corroborated.)

The Wang Jinzhi murder case appears to be the novel’s invention: no documented Shanghai crime by that name could be found in the reference record. Its setting, though, is real. Taikoo (太古) is Butterfield & Swire, whose China Navigation Company, founded in 1872, ran passenger-and-cargo steamers on the Yangtze between Shanghai and Hankou; a ship’s chafang (茶房), here rendered ‘steward,’ was the attendant who waited on passengers, and a trusted head steward carrying valuables upriver is true to the trade. (The case is uncorroborated; the Taikoo steamer trade is corroborated.)

The bank’s deliberately canted corner and corner-facing door reflect fengshui (风水, ‘geomancy’), the traditional art of siting a building and its openings to court good fortune — a consideration common even in the design of modern Shanghai commercial buildings. (Texture.)

ch16.anchor: the Shanghai households open their doors and set off a string of
ch16.note: The door-opening crackers (开门炮仗) are the New Year custom of letting off a string of firecrackers the moment a household first opens its door on New Year’s morning, to see out the old year, drive off bad luck and open the new year auspiciously; the louder the burst, the better the omen. (Corroborated.)

ch16.anchor: the internal investigation room for family discipline
ch16.note: To be handed to the internal investigation room for family discipline is a threat of the secret service’s own private punishment of its members — 家法, ‘family law,’ the discipline a clan or gang metes out to its own, outside any court. (Texture.)

ch17.note: The Nationalist gendarmerie (宪兵, military police) were a real standing force with police powers, an ordinary presence in 1930s Shanghai; armored cars (铁甲车) were likewise real, some built at the Shanghai Arsenal in 1929–30 with mounted machine guns. A garrison unit lending one to the secret police for such an operation is plausible for the period. (Corroborated.)

ch17.anchor: the Ministry of Finance's public-bond business
ch17.note: The detail hints at the power behind the small bank. That a ‘Mr. Song’ (宋) should have an all-important elder brother, and the bank a share of the Ministry of Finance’s bond issues, invites the reader to think of the Soong (宋) family, whose T. V. Soong (宋子文) was the Nationalist finance minister of just these years (1928–1933); the novel leaves the connection unspoken. The real Zhonghui Bank was in fact the Green Gang boss Du Yuesheng’s (see the note on the bank). (T. V. Soong and the finance ministry are corroborated; the identification of ‘Mr. Song’ is the reader’s inference, not stated.)

The Nanshi police were real. Shanghai had three separate forces — the Settlement’s Municipal Police, the French Concession police, and a Chinese municipal force over the Chinese-administered districts, headquartered in Nanshi (the Shanghai Municipal Public Security Bureau, so named from 1930). That the car belongs to the Chinese-city police, and that there might be Communists inside it, turns on this jurisdictional patchwork; the exact station name is the novel’s. (Corroborated.)

The Three Principles of the People (三民主义) — Nationalism, Democracy (people’s rights) and the People’s Livelihood — were Sun Yat-sen’s doctrine, given definitive form in his 1924 Guangzhou lectures, and the official ideology of the Nationalist party and state. Ye Qinian’s creed, that Communism is to be beaten not by killing but by converting minds to the Three Principles, is exactly the regime’s official line. (Corroborated.)

Professor Tao of Central University is most likely Tao Xisheng (陶希圣, 1899–1988), who joined National Central University in Nanjing in 1931 and was known as a theorist of the Three Principles, and who later ghostwrote Chiang Kai-shek’s China’s Destiny (1943). But in the early 1930s Tao was chiefly a social historian, and had earlier belonged to an anti-Chiang faction; his hard anti-Communist role crystallized only later, so a specific 1933 anti-Communist primer by him is not documented. The recommendation reads as the novel projecting his later authority back onto this scene. (The professor is corroborated; the book is uncorroborated.)

ch18.note: The French Concession Municipal Council (公董局, Conseil d’administration municipale) governed Shanghai’s French Concession — a separate authority from the Shanghai Municipal Council (工部局) that ran the International Settlement. Its writ ran only to the north bank of the Zhaojiabang; the creek’s south bank was Chinese-administered ground, which is why the firm’s coal yard there lay beyond the reach of the Concession police. (Corroborated.)

A clue that works only in the written script. The dying Old Fang scrawls a half-formed 山 (shan, ‘mountain’); the traitor’s surname, Cui (崔), is written with exactly that element, 山, set atop the graph. The unfinished character therefore points to Cui Wentai. English can report the stroke but not the naming, which is why it needs a note.

ch18.anchor: the bone of a rebel in his skull
ch18.note: Wei Dafu reads Cui Wentai’s face by the old art of physiognomy. To have ‘cheekbones you can see from behind’ (脑后见萶) marked a man as treacherous and ungrateful; the bone of a rebel (反骨, literally a ‘bone of rebellion’) alludes to the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, in which Zhuge Liang, spying such a bone at the back of the general Wei Yan’s skull, foretells that he will one day turn traitor. (A real physiognomic tradition and a real literary allusion; the reading of Cui’s face is the novel’s.)

ch18.anchor: the counter-revolutionary governments of Ninghan and Ningyue
ch18.note: Lin Shi compresses several years of Nationalist consolidation. The Ninghan (宁汉) split was the 1927 rupture between Chiang Kai-shek’s Nanjing (宁) government and the Wuhan (汉) government under Wang Jingwei; after Wang broke with the Communists the two reconciled, the Ninghan merger of September 1927. The Ningyue (宁粤) confrontation was the breakaway Canton (粤) government of 1931, later brought back into the fold. (Corroborated.)

ch18.anchor: the thirteenth card in the deck
ch18.note: The operation’s code names are playing cards. Lin Shi’s, Laokai (老开), the text glosses as the King — the thirteenth card of a suit, ace through king. It is of a piece with the book’s running motif of games of chance: the dice of the opening chapters, the ‘game of chess’ the whole plan is likened to. (The novel’s device.)

ch18.anchor: even a film studio had put up its sound stages nearby
ch18.note: A real film-studio district lay on this southwestern fringe of the Concessions: the Lianhua company (联华影业公司, from 1930) had its photographic studio on Caoxi Road in the Xujiahui area, the site later taken over by the Shanghai Film Studio. (The studio district is corroborated; the novel names no particular studio.)

ch18.anchor: squatted on the waste ground nearby and thrown up shacks
ch18.note: These squatter shacks are the penghu (棚户, ‘shack households’) settlements that grew on Shanghai’s margins as country people fleeing the lower-Yangtze floods poured into the city; thrown up first of planks and then of cinder-and-mud brick on waste ground the authorities ignored, they housed much of the city’s unskilled labor. (Corroborated.)

ch18.anchor: from Rue Père Robert into Xujiahui Road
ch18.note: Rue Père Robert (金神父路) was a French Concession street, laid out about 1907 and named for a French missionary priest, Father Robert; it became Ruijin Er Road (瑞金二路) in 1943 and keeps that name today. (Corroborated.)

Gujiazhai Park (顾家宅公园), the ‘French Park,’ opened on Bastille Day 1909 in the French Concession, laid out in formal French-garden style and at first reserved for French residents; it was renamed Fuxing Park (复兴公园) in 1946, the name it bears today. The ‘iron gate into the French Concession’ mentioned below is the boundary between the Concession and the Chinese city. (Corroborated.)

ch19.note: February (二月) is a real novella by Rou Shi (柔石, pen name of Zhao Pingfu, 1902–1931), published by the Chunchao Book Company in Shanghai in November 1929 with a short preface by Lu Xun, who had edited it. Its hero, the schoolteacher Xiao Jianqiu, befriends a young widow whose husband was killed in battle and who is left with two small children — the book Ling Wen describes. Rou Shi belonged to the League of Left-Wing Writers and was one of its Five Martyrs, secretly shot by the Nationalists at Longhua on February 7, 1931 — the same killing ground, and all but the same month, that give this chapter and this novel their weight. Lu Xun’s memorial essay ‘In Memory of the Forgotten’ was written in February 1933, just when A Thousand Li is set. (Corroborated.)

ch19.anchor: the woodcut design was of the plainest
ch19.note: The novel makes the jacket a woodcut — a river bearing leaves, rain and human faces. The historical first edition of February in fact carried a line drawing by Tao Yuanqing (陶元庆, 1893–1929), among his last works, not a woodcut; the woodcut art Lu Xun championed came through his Morning Flower Society, not this cover. The image here is the novel’s own, and its drifting faces read as a quiet figure for the drowned dead the book commemorates. (The woodcut cover is uncorroborated; the design is the novel’s.)

ch19.anchor: a lawyer from the Relief Society
ch19.note: The Relief Society (济难会) was the China Relief Society, founded under Communist leadership in 1925 and reorganized as the China Red Aid Society (中国革命互济会) in 1929, the Chinese arm of the international Red Aid movement. It relieved the families of arrested and executed revolutionaries and, exactly as here, retained sympathetic lawyers to bail comrades out of prison. The Nationalist government banned it in 1934. (Corroborated.)

ch19.anchor: a cat curled at the stove
ch19.note: A cat curled at the stove renders weizaomao (牢灼猫), a Wu-dialect phrase — a cat drowsing at the kitchen fire — for a listless, spiritless creature. Wei Dafu resents the label; Chen Qianli turns it into praise a moment later, when at the crucial hour ‘the stove-cat turns into a tiger.’ (An idiom of the Shanghai region.)

Nine-dragon shells and meteor-crackers (九龙, 流星) are evocative names from the long Chinese repertoire of fireworks — ‘meteors’ for a rising streak of sparks, ‘nine dragons’ echoing the old set-piece 九龙取水 (‘nine dragons drawing water’) — descriptive effect-names rather than fixed modern product types. (The festival custom and the ‘meteor’ type are corroborated; the names are traditional and literary.)

ch20.note: Dashatou Station (大沙头站), built in 1911, was the Guangzhou terminus of the Canton–Kowloon Railway (广九铁路), the line to Hong Kong, and the city’s eastern railhead in this era; it was renamed Guangzhou East Station in 1947. Arriving from Hong Kong, Ling Wen and Yi Junnian would indeed have come in here. (Corroborated.)

ch20.anchor: Comrade Deng Zhongxia had lectured there
ch20.note: Deng Zhongxia (邓中夏, 1894–1933) was a founding leader of the Chinese labor movement and, with Su Zhaozheng, a chief organizer of the Canton–Hong Kong Strike; the strike committee ran worker-education bodies, a Labour College (劳动学院) among them, at which he lectured. He was arrested in Shanghai and executed by the Nationalists at Yuhuatai, Nanjing, in September 1933, months after this novel’s events. (Deng and the Labour College are corroborated; siting the college on the fourth floor of the Nanhua Building is the novel’s detail, unconfirmed in the record.)

ch20.anchor: Under Chen Jitang's rule of Guangdong
ch20.note: Chen Jitang (陈济棉, 1890–1954), the militarist called the ‘King of the Southern Sky,’ governed Guangdong all but independently of Nanjing from about 1929 to 1936, so his rule in early 1933 is accurate. His regime pressed a conservative, Confucian-revival social order, down to dress codes for women, which bears out the novel’s picture of a place where a man and woman sharing one rickshaw would draw the eye. (Corroborated.)
